ai.definition: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses the temperature difference between warm surface water and colder deep water to generate electricity. It operates on the principle of using this temperature gradient to drive a heat engine.
ai.howItWorks: Warm seawater from the surface is drawn into a heat exchanger, where it boils a low-boiling-point working fluid (such as ammonia or propane). The vaporized fluid drives a turbine connected to a generator. Cold water from deeper in the ocean is then used to condense the vapor back into a liquid, which is recirculated through the system.
ai.problemSolved: OTEC addresses the need for reliable and constant baseload power generation, particularly in tropical regions where the temperature difference between surface and deep waters is significant. It provides a zero-emission alternative to fossil fuels without relying on intermittent sources like solar or wind.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves constructing OTEC plants with heat exchangers, turbines, generators, and cooling systems. These components are typically made from durable materials suitable for marine environments, such as stainless steel and aluminum alloys.
ai.buildProcess: OTEC plants require careful site selection due to the need for consistent temperature gradients. The build process includes designing and constructing the plant, installing heat exchangers, turbines, and electrical systems, followed by testing and commissioning.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial capital investment, marine construction costs, energy storage requirements (for open-cycle OTEC), and maintenance expenses. The cost of materials, labor, and environmental impact assessments also contribute to the overall expense.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: OTEC is expected to grow as technology improves and more projects are developed in suitable locations. However, it faces challenges such as high initial costs and limited geographical applicability.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but generally require environmental impact assessments and compliance with maritime safety standards. Incentives for renewable energy may also be available in some regions to support OTEC projects.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include potential impacts on marine ecosystems, particularly if not managed properly during construction and operation. Technical risks involve the complexity of operating in a marine environment and ensuring long-term reliability of components.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited due to high initial costs and lower power generation compared to some other renewable technologies. However, it could become more viable as technology improves and economies of scale are achieved.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on reducing costs through technological advancements, improving efficiency, and expanding the range of applications for OTEC beyond electricity generation (e.g., desalination).

glossary.def: A device that transfers heat from one fluid to another without the fluids mixing.
The substance used in a thermodynamic cycle to absorb and transfer energy, such as ammonia or propane.
An OTEC system where the working fluid is continuously recycled without being released into the environment.

subsystems.name: Cold-water pipe
subsystems.role: draws near-freezing water from about 1,000 m depth, the single hardest piece of marine engineering in the plant.

subsystems.name: Heat exchangers
subsystems.role: evaporate the working fluid with warm surface water and condense it with cold deep water.

subsystems.name: Power cycle
subsystems.role: turns the vapour pressure difference into rotation.
parts: ammonia working-fluid loop (closed cycle) or flash evaporator and vacuum vessel (open cycle)

subsystems.name: Seawater handling
subsystems.role: moves enormous volumes of warm and cold water through the plant.

subsystems.name: Platform and mooring
subsystems.role: holds the plant and pipe in place through storms.
parts: floating hull or land-based site at the shelf edge

subsystems.name: Power export
subsystems.role: sends electricity to a grid or uses it on board.

buildSteps.title: Find the thermal resource
buildSteps.detail: Survey a site with a year-round temperature difference of about 20 °C between the surface and 1,000 m, ideally where the seabed drops away steeply so the cold-water pipe can be short.

buildSteps.title: Design the cold-water pipe
buildSteps.detail: Size a pipe a metre or more across and up to a kilometre long, and work out how it survives bending, currents and waves without buckling or fatigue.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the heat exchangers
buildSteps.detail: Build thousands of square metres of corrosion-resistant surface area per megawatt — the largest single cost — with surfaces that resist marine growth.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the plant
buildSteps.detail: Either build onshore at the shelf edge or construct on a floating hull or converted ship, installing pumps, turbine and ammonia loop.

buildSteps.title: Install the pipe
buildSteps.detail: Tow the pipe to site, sink it under controlled flooding or hang it from the platform — a marine operation comparable to installing an oil riser.

buildSteps.title: Commission the cycle
buildSteps.detail: Start the turbine on ammonia vapour, purge non-condensable air, and tune pumping rates so net output is as high as possible.

buildSteps.title: Operate and maintain
buildSteps.detail: Continuously monitor biofouling, pipe fatigue and heat-exchanger performance; pumping and cleaning loads consume a large share of gross output.

prerequisites.tech: Large-diameter deep-sea pipe and riser engineering
prerequisites.why: mostly borrowed from oil and gas; OTEC-scale cold-water pipes have only been demonstrated at roughly a metre diameter and a few hundred metres.
heat transfer must stay high for decades in warm, biologically rich seawater.
ammonia and organic Rankine cycles are mature in refrigeration and geothermal plants.

pathway.milestone: small demonstration plants of roughly 100 kW, such as those run at ocean-energy test sites in Hawaii and Japan since the 1980s and 1990s
pathway.unlocks: proof of the cycle and of cold-water delivery, but no commercial output.

pathway.milestone: a multi-megawatt pilot with an integrated kilometre-scale cold-water pipe at a steep-shelf site
pathway.unlocks: real cost and reliability data for the pipe and heat exchangers.

pathway.milestone: plants that sell co-products as well as electricity — desalinated water, chilled water for air conditioning, aquaculture
pathway.unlocks: a business case on tropical islands where diesel power is expensive.

pathway.milestone: floating plants of tens of megawatts, mass-produced and moored offshore
pathway.unlocks: firm, weather-independent baseload for island grids, and possibly hydrogen or ammonia export.
